title: Faster Chaitin-like Register Allocation via Grammatical Decompositions of Control-Flow Graphs
problem: Register allocation via graph coloring (Chaitin-style) is NP-hard in general, but practical compilers rely on heuristics that do not exploit the sparse, structured nature of real program control-flow graphs (CFGs). This leads to suboptimal allocation or unnecessary spills in programs with structured control flow.
method: The paper formalizes the sparsity of structured program CFGs using graph-theoretic parameters (treewidth, pathwidth) and introduces a grammatical decomposition—parsing the CFG into a tree decomposition. Register allocation is then solved efficiently via dynamic programming on this tree decomposition, yielding a parameterized algorithm whose complexity scales with the treewidth of the CFG rather than graph size alone. This exploits the observation that real programs' CFGs have small treewidth, making previously intractable exact or near-exact coloring feasible.

title: Fast On-device LLM Inference with NPUs
problem: On-device LLM inference on mobile NPUs incurs unacceptably high latency, particularly during the prefill stage, because existing NPU programming models are not designed to efficiently map the irregular, attention-heavy computation patterns of LLMs. Even mobile-sized models (e.g., Gemma-2B) run too slowly for interactive tasks such as screen UI understanding.
method: The system analyzes the NPU execution bottlenecks of mobile LLMs and redesigns the inference pipeline to exploit NPU-specific parallelism. It introduces operator fusion and tiling strategies tailored to NPU dataflow constraints, and reorders computation to overlap NPU and CPU execution. The approach targets the prefill stage specifically, batching token processing to amortize NPU invocation overhead and restructuring attention kernels to fit the NPU's fixed-function units.

title: Adaptive CHERI Compartmentalization for Heterogeneous Accelerators
problem: Hardware accelerators in heterogeneous systems lack fine-grained memory protection: IOMMU-based isolation operates at page granularity, leaving intra-page accesses unprotected, while per-accelerator memory safety modifications require significant engineering effort and do not scale across diverse accelerator types.
method: CapChecker is an adaptive hardware interface inserted between CHERI-unaware accelerators and the system memory bus. It imports capability metadata from the CPU's CHERI register file and enforces pointer-level bounds and permission checks on every memory access issued by the accelerator, without modifying the accelerator architecture itself. The interface interposes on the accelerator's memory request channel, decodes the capability tag and bounds from the CPU-managed capability table, and raises a fault on any out-of-bounds or permission-violating access. Capability grants from the CPU are communicated through a lightweight descriptor mechanism that maps accelerator DMA addresses to CHERI capabilities.

title: Drishti: Do Not Forget Slicing While Designing Last-Level Cache Replacement Policies for Many-Core Systems
problem: State-of-the-art LLC replacement policies (Hawkeye, Mockingjay) use a per-slice sampled cache and a per-slice reuse predictor that make myopic decisions based only on accesses to a single slice, unaware of global reuse behavior across all LLC slices in many-core systems; additionally, per-slice sampled cache sets receive insufficient LLC misses to drive accurate replacement decisions.
method: Drishti proposes two enhancements to existing LLC replacement policies for sliced LLCs: (1) a per-core global reuse predictor where each core's predictor is trained on all accesses by that core across all LLC slices—achieving global reuse awareness without centralized inter-slice interconnect traffic—combined with a local (per-slice) sampled cache that remains slice-local; (2) a per-slice dynamic sampled cache that adaptively expands the set of LLC sets used for sampling to improve the sample quality and ensure adequate miss coverage per slice. Evaluated by augmenting Hawkeye and Mockingjay on 4, 16, and 32-core systems with 8, 32, and 64 MB sliced LLCs.

title: DataMaestro: A Versatile and Efficient Data Streaming Engine Bringing Decoupled Memory Access To Dataflow Accelerators
problem: DNN inference on dataflow accelerators faces performance bottlenecks from data movement; accelerators lack decoupled access/execute architectures to mitigate memory access inefficiency and bank conflicts.
method: DataMaestro is a programmable data streaming unit supporting flexible access patterns, fine-grained prefetch and bank-conflict mitigation through dynamic addressing mode switching, and on-the-fly data manipulation to reduce memory footprints. Integrated with Tensor Core-like GeMM and quantization accelerators on RISC-V host with FPGA prototype and VLSI synthesis validation.

title: Late Breaking Results: A Fast Nearest Neighbor Search Acceleration for 3D Point Cloud
problem: K-Nearest Neighbors search in point clouds requires expensive Euclidean distance calculations over large candidate sets, limiting throughput on edge devices and real-time applications.
method: Uses locality-sensitive E2LSH partitioning to pre-filter candidate points, employs a precomparator module to reduce candidate search space further, and optimizes Euclidean distance computation to minimize expensive calculations while maintaining high precision.

title: AARC: Automated Affinity-aware Resource Configuration for Serverless Workflows
problem: Traditional serverless resource allocation couples CPU and memory, creating suboptimal provisioning for diverse workloads. Decoupling improves flexibility but introduces a massive configuration space that is difficult to optimize for complex workflows.
method: AARC uses a Graph-Centric Scheduler to identify critical paths in workflow DAGs, then applies a Priority Configurator using priority scheduling techniques to optimize CPU-memory allocation. The approach reduces search time by focusing on high-impact configuration decisions and maintaining SLO compliance.

title: FlexStep: Enabling Flexible Error Detection in Multi/Many-core Real-time Systems
problem: Traditional error detection (e.g., LockStep) requires pre-configured checker cores and static regions, causing over-provisioning and reducing real-time performance in systems with mixed reliability requirements.
method: FlexStep integrates hardware microarchitecture supporting dynamic core reconfiguration with OS scheduling layer; enables asynchronous, preemptive error detection via lightweight hardware support and OS-level task scheduling policies.

title: Curvilinear Optical Proximity Correction via Cardinal Spline
problem: Optical proximity correction (OPC) must handle curvilinear mask patterns with complex geometry; traditional OPC approaches struggle with curvature while maintaining mask rule checking compliance.
method: Proposes curvilinear OPC framework using cardinal splines to represent mask patterns through control points; iteratively adjusts control points guided by lithography simulation; develops comprehensive MRC checking methods for width, space, area, and curvature; designs algorithms to fit inverse lithography technique (ILT) results and resolve MRC violations.

title: Towards End-to-End Optimization of LLM-based Applications with Ayo
problem: LLM-based applications consist of both LLM and non-LLM components whose combined end-to-end latency is not jointly optimized by existing frameworks, which use coarse-grained task-module orchestration that confines optimizations within individual modules.
method: Ayo introduces a fine-grained, end-to-end workflow optimizer for LLM-based applications that breaks down application pipelines below the task-module boundary, enabling cross-module scheduling decisions. The system models the full application DAG and applies joint optimization of LLM inference scheduling alongside non-LLM compute stages to minimize overall pipeline latency.

title: GraphFI: An Efficient Fault Injection Framework for Graph Processing on GPGPUs
problem: Existing fault injection methods ignore graph-specific execution paradigms (iterations, vertices, error propagation), producing inaccurate system error resilience characterization and blind fault injection trials that are computationally expensive.
method: GraphFI exploits three graph-specific properties: iteration-driven FI (selecting representative iterations with similar active vertex sets), topology-driven FI (identifying resilience-similarity communities and testing representative vertices), and monotonicity-driven FI (using fault monotonic properties to predict severe error boundaries). Merging all three approaches reduces fault site space by up to 100x.

title: Late Breaking Results: Encoder-Decoder Generative Diffusion Transformer Towards Push-Button Analog IC Sizing
problem: Analog IC sizing relies on time-consuming optimization-based methods that lack scalability and generalization to unseen performance targets.
method: Encoder-decoder diffusion transformer (attention-based generative model) solves inverse analog sizing problem by sampling accurate solutions at push-button speed, trained on performance targets to generalize beyond training set.

title: CROSS: Compiler-Driven Optimization of Sparse DNNs Using Sparse/Dense Computation Kernels
problem: Exploiting DNN weight sparsity on GPUs is hindered by the overhead of index-based encoding/decoding required by sparse formats, making sparse computation kernels slower than dense kernels even at high sparsity ratios.
method: CROSS is an end-to-end compilation framework that analyzes parameter distribution locality to identify regions where dense computation remains efficient. It decomposes sparse DNN workloads into multiple components across different sparsity levels and maps each component to either a specialized sparse kernel or a high-performance dense kernel. A novel sparse graph translation technique transforms the sparse computation graph into a form compatible with dense computation kernels, reconciling the sparse DNN computation with optimized BLAS-level dense routines on GPU. The framework accommodates various sparsity patterns (unstructured, structured, N:M) and optimization techniques.

title: LightRIM: Light Runtime Integrity Measurement for Linux Kernels in Embedded Applications
problem: Linux kernel security modules provide integrity monitoring but consume substantial computational resources, making them unsuitable for resource-limited embedded systems like autonomous vehicles and robots.
method: LightRIM performs two-stage hashing on monitored kernel objects and uses event-triggered measurement tied to security value changes. A heuristic algorithm maximizes attack detection rate within CPU budget constraints via randomized measurement intervals to mitigate TOCTOU vulnerabilities.

title: Earth+: On-Board Satellite Imagery Compression Leveraging Historical Earth Observations
problem: Satellite downlink capacity is so limited that over 90% of captured earth-observation images are never downloaded; existing on-board compression techniques treat each image independently and cannot exploit the rich temporal and spatial redundancy available across an entire satellite constellation.
method: Earth+ implements a change-detection-based compression pipeline on the satellite. Ground stations upload recently captured reference images from other satellites in the same constellation to each on-board satellite via the uplink. On-board processing compares each newly captured image against the latest matching reference image and transmits only the changed regions (delta encoding). The system manages reference image currency and on-board storage to ensure that references are temporally close to the captured images, maximizing delta sparsity and thus compression.

title: BrokenSleep: Remote Power Timing Attack Exploiting Processor Idle States
problem: Modern processors support multiple C-state (idle) levels with different wake-up latencies; an attacker can remotely detect which C-state a victim processor core is in by measuring network response timing, enabling covert and side-channel communication across nodes without requiring co-location on the same machine.
method: BrokenSleep exploits the deterministic wake-up latency differences between processor C-states (C0 active, C1/C1E/C6 sleep) to encode information in the timing of network responses from a victim server. The attacker sends network requests and measures response latency; the victim's current C-state (determined by its workload idle pattern) is deduced from the latency profile. Both covert channel (data exfiltration across security boundaries without direct network access) and side-channel (keystroke timing inference) variants are demonstrated. The attack affects both Intel and ARM processors, exploiting standard ACPI power management without any microarchitectural vulnerability.
